name: Vera Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I climb into a haul truck at the big mine just before six and take rock from the cut to the crusher. I joined this crew late, so I still ask the experienced drivers about a rough turn or a strange sound. I like a clean run and the pay is better than I made in the shop. The shifts leave my knees stiff, and my partner Ken is usually finishing supper when I get home. Our children are grown; we aren't paying school bills, but we're trying to keep the house in good shape before retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a computer can make the forms shorter if it likes, but someone still has to move the rock. I don't see a reason to turn a steady shift upside down for a small saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I hope the mine keeps taking beginners like me. I have more than six months of living costs put away, but I only recently got the higher wage here and want a few more years of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the same route and keep asking Mara, the lead driver, when a truck sounds wrong. In the first year I'd have Ken and me review the roof estimate before we spend on the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I'm settled. The knee bothers me more than the little bit of AI on this card, though I wouldn't ignore a change to the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ken about the roof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Ken the roof comes before new cupboards. We can pay for it without borrowing if we stick to the plan we already made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does being newer matter if routine tasks change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because I'm still proving I can handle a loaded truck safely. A form filled by a machine doesn't teach me where the soft shoulder is.

say: I would keep **moving rock** and treat shorter forms as a small convenience.
I would ask the crew to keep **safety judgement** with drivers.
think: I want several more years of the mine’s **higher wage**.
My **savings** cover months, but I am still establishing myself on this crew.
do: Keep driving the **haul route** and checking odd sounds with the lead driver.
Review the **roof estimate** before approving new kitchen spending.
feel: I feel **settled**, with my knee more present than AI.
S0.quote: A form filled by a machine doesn't teach me where the soft shoulder is.
fieldNote: Her interest in the **mine wage** reflects a late start on this crew, not current financial strain.
She separates routine paperwork from **driving skill** and measures security against the roof repair.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck on the cut-to-crusher route
Review the roof estimate before paying for new cupboards

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the planners can use their new software, but they ought to ask drivers before changing the run. I'd also tell the younger ones to learn the equipment, because a screen won't spot every bad patch of road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Behind that, I worry the office will trim shifts when buying and schedules get easier. Plenty of mines hire drivers nearby, yet I wouldn't enjoy starting over at 58, and a junior worker could be first off a roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the shift boss which driving hours are actually forecast and check the notices for other haul jobs every month. If my hours fell in the first year, Ken and I would postpone the kitchen and use the savings only for ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy when I picture a thinner roster. I've changed jobs before, but I wanted this one to be the last full-time job before retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask first about hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my shift boss on a quiet Thursday, not raise it in front of the whole crew. I want a number of shifts, not a speech about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident in the machine but worried about the office.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck is work I can point to. The office decides whether there are four drivers on a shift or three, and I won't know until the list goes up.

say: I would urge **planners** to hear drivers before changing routes.
I would tell younger drivers to keep learning the **equipment**.
think: My junior place could mean **fewer shifts** if scheduling gets leaner.
My local job options exist, but another **fresh start** at 58 is hard.
do: Ask the shift boss for the forecast number of **driving shifts**.
Check local **haul jobs** monthly and postpone the kitchen if hours fall.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the roster and protective of my final working years.
S1.quote: The office decides whether there are four drivers on a shift or three, and I won't know until the list goes up.
fieldNote: She sees near-term risk through **staffing decisions** rather than a robot taking her seat.
Her willingness to check **vacancies** is pragmatic despite a strong preference for familiar work.

steps.text: Ask the shift boss for the coming driving-hours forecast
Check nearby haul-driver vacancies each month
Postpone kitchen spending if driving hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that full thinking AI in 2028 is a management problem first and a driving problem when robots arrive around 2031. I would ask for a straight timetable, because a person can't plan retirement around rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the mine could put smarter dispatch in quickly, and the boss might cut a junior driver before the robots are ready. If that happens at 60, my savings buy time but don't replace the wages I counted on for the house and retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written estimate of our shifts this winter and price the roof now, while I still have full pay. If a driving notice came in 2028, I'd apply to the two neighbouring mines; in 2029 I'd keep doing paid truck shifts wherever I could get them and stop the kitchen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That makes my chest tight. I know I can drive, but two years is hardly time for a newcomer to become the one everyone keeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Ken we should finish the roof and leave the kitchen as it is. Our grown children can visit without shiny cupboards, and we shouldn't ask them to carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a new system if they offered it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the required safety briefing, of course. I'm not signing up for a course on a promise that it will protect a truck job after 2031.

say: I would demand a **timetable** for dispatch changes and later robots.
I would tell the crew that driving lasts beyond **2028**, though staffing may change earlier.
think: I could lose shifts before robots if **dispatch** reduces the roster.
My savings buy time but cannot replace the **wages** I expected.
do: Request a written **shift forecast** and price the roof while full pay continues.
Apply to **nearby mines** after a driving notice and halt the kitchen renovation.
feel: I feel **tight-chested** about being a new driver with little time to establish myself.
S2.quote: Our grown children can visit without shiny cupboards, and we shouldn't ask them to carry us.
fieldNote: She distinguishes the **2028 desk change** from the 2031 hands-on threat and anticipates an earlier roster cut.
Family pride shapes her **spending decision**; she would rather delay the kitchen than lean on grown children.

steps.text: Ask the mine for a written forecast of driving shifts
Apply to the two neighbouring mines if driving shifts are cut
Stop the kitchen renovation if a driving notice arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the mine enough time to be honest about where the trucks are going. Full thinking AI in 2031 might change dispatch first, and robots around 2034 are the real question for my seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the thinking system arrives and 66 when the robots are due. That puts retirement closer, but it doesn't tell me whether I can afford to stop driving at 63; I haven't assumed a pension will cover the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep this job now and ask Ken to sit down with our actual spending and savings this month. By 2032, if the roster shrinks, I'd apply for a driving job at the neighbouring stone pit; in the first year after robots arrive I'd take paid driving shifts if any remain and delay any retirement decision until we know the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed than with the two-year picture. I still hate imagining my last years of work decided by a machine purchase I have no say in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would settle the retirement question?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need to know what our monthly bills are after the roof is done. We have a cushion, but I won't call it retirement money until we've put the figures beside a realistic wage gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would another mine take a 66-year-old driver?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I won't pretend it will. The stone pit has hired older drivers before, so I would ask there while I still have a current safety record.

say: I would ask the mine for an honest **truck timetable**.
I would explain that dispatch changes in **2031** precede robots around 2034.
think: I would be **63** at thinking AI and 66 at the robot date.
My retirement date depends on **bills and wages**, not age alone.
do: Review **household spending** with Ken and continue paid driving.
Apply at the **stone pit** if the mine roster shrinks.
feel: I feel **less rushed** but dislike depending on the mine’s purchase decision.
S3.quote: I won't call it retirement money until we've put the figures beside a realistic wage gap.
fieldNote: She does not confuse a substantial **savings cushion** with guaranteed retirement income.
The longer runway lets her use **household figures** and a nearby stone pit as options, while preserving paid work.

steps.text: Review monthly bills and savings with partner Ken
Apply for a driving job at the stone pit if shifts shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade is enough time for a mine to show its hand instead of whispering about robots. Thinking AI in 2036 will change the office, but the trucks still need drivers until about 2039 on this card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when the thinking AI arrives and 71 at the robot date. If my health and the pay hold up, I might have stopped full-time driving before then, but I won't claim that is settled today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the truck job as long as it's safe for me and worthwhile for us, then review our retirement numbers each year with Ken. In 2037 I'd check whether the mine still wants paid drivers and decide from our actual bills whether to reduce shifts; when robots arrive, I'd leave only if we can live on what we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fairly calm about a change that far away. My knee may make the decision before any robot does, and that is something I already discuss with Ken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the long warning change spending now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We still need to do the roof, and I wouldn't put that off for a 2039 robot. I would keep the kitchen modest because I prefer money in reserve anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you work past 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A safe truck, a decent roster and bills that still need a wage. I won't drive heavy equipment to prove a point if my reactions get slow.

say: I would ask for clear **robot plans** over the decade.
I would remind the crew that trucks still need drivers until around **2039**.
think: I may have left full-time driving by **71**, though my finances are not settled.
My **health** may decide the timing before a robot does.
do: Keep **driving** while safe and review retirement figures annually with Ken.
Check for **paid shifts** in 2037 before deciding whether to reduce hours.
feel: I feel **fairly calm** with a decade to judge both work and health.
S4.quote: My knee may make the decision before any robot does, and that is something I already discuss with Ken.
fieldNote: A decade makes the **robot date** less immediate than her knee and household budget.
She remains open to **paid work** through 2037 and refuses to call retirement certain without figures.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck while reactions remain safe
Review retirement spending and savings with Ken each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could be pushed off a roster before I've had a fair stretch on this wage. A written shift timetable from the mine, with proper notice before cuts, would help me make decisions about the roof and applications.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to a driver who starts late. I know the older hands have earned their place, A newer worker my age has fewer years to recover from a bad decision.

headlineQuote: A newer worker my age has fewer years to recover from a bad decision.
portrait: Vera is a **58-year-old junior driver** at a large mine, earning more than in her former shop job.
She has a strong **savings cushion**, grown children and a partner, but wants more paid years before retirement.
She trusts **driving experience** and dislikes unproven technology; her knee is an existing concern.
She fears **roster cuts** most and uses nearby vacancies and postponed spending as practical safeguards.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because dispatch cuts could threaten a late start on higher pay.
whatWouldHelp: A written **shift timetable** and advance notice of cuts would let her plan spending and job applications.
